solutions.title: Fetal Health Risk Detection & Clustering
solutions.description: An unsupervised pipeline that flags at-risk fetal heart-rate patterns and groups 2,126 real cardiotocogram recordings into risk tiers — without ever seeing the clinical diagnosis. Isolation Forest anomalies concentrate 12x more in cases obstetricians independently classified as pathological (48.9% vs. 4.1%), and K-Means recovers a high-risk cluster where pathological cases outnumber normal ones. A real early-warning signal, built entirely from the signal itself.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: Real clinical monitoring produces a dense stream of numbers per patient — heart rate, variability, contractions — that even trained clinicians have to read holistically, in real time. Could an algorithm that never sees the diagnosis still learn to spot what actually matters?

narrative.label: The Data
narrative.text: 2,126 real cardiotocogram recordings, each independently classified Normal, Suspect, or Pathologic by a consensus of expert obstetricians (Ayres-de-Campos & Bernardes, 2000). That diagnosis was set aside completely during modeling — it comes back later, only to grade the work, never to train on.

narrative.label: Finding What's Unusual
narrative.text: An Isolation Forest was trained on the 20 raw measured features per recording — never the diagnosis — and asked one question: which recordings look structurally different from the rest? The red points below are everything it flagged.
narrative.caption: Isolation Forest anomalies, 2,126 recordings in PCA space — the model never saw a diagnosis.

narrative.label: Did It Actually Work?
narrative.text: Only after the model made its decisions did we compare its flags against the real diagnoses. Recordings doctors called Pathologic were flagged anomalous 12x more often than recordings they called Normal — a gap this wide doesn't happen by chance.
narrative.caption: Anomaly rate by real clinical diagnosis, checked after the fact.

narrative.label: Grouping by Risk
narrative.text: A second, independent model — K-Means — sorted every recording into one of three groups, again with zero access to the diagnosis. One group came out almost entirely Normal. Another inverted the dataset's own risk ratio: inside that one cluster, Pathologic cases actually outnumber Normal ones.
narrative.caption: K-Means (k=3) — real diagnosis composition per cluster, revealed only afterward.

narrative.label: An Honest Extra Check
narrative.text: We also compared the flagged anomalies against a real external clinical threshold — ACOG's normal fetal heart-rate range. They barely overlapped. That's not a failure: it shows this multivariate model catches risk patterns a single clinical rule alone would miss, instead of just rediscovering what a simpler check already knows.

narrative.label: Why It Matters
narrative.text: None of this replaces a doctor. What it demonstrates is that a fully unsupervised model, given only the raw signal, independently rediscovers real clinical risk — a legitimate, honest early-warning layer worth building on, not a black box asked to take over.

study.code_spotlight:
# 1. Anomaly detection — unsupervised, never sees NSP
iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, contamination=0.08, random_state=42)
df['anomaly'] = iso.fit_predict(X_scaled) == -1

# 2. Clustering — validated post-hoc against the real diagnosis
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42)
df['cluster'] = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# 3. External validation — did the model rediscover real clinical risk?
pd.crosstab(df['anomaly'], df['NSP_label'], normalize='columns') * 100
# Pathologic: 48.9% flagged anomalous  |  Normal: 4.1% flagged anomalous

solutions.title: Automated Mission Planning for Autonomous Rovers
solutions.description: A PDDL domain and optimal planner (Fast Downward, A* + LM-Cut, run in a Singularity container) that plans multi-stop rover routes over a directional path network — provably optimal every time, verified independently against a second planner. The same domain.pddl handles three growing scenarios without a single line changed, and in the hardest one the planner independently chose the closer of two labs for each delivery.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: A rover has already excavated two mineral samples at two different sites. Bad weather stopped it from moving them. Plan the route that gets both to the analysis lab — over a path network where some roads only go one way.

narrative.label: Proving the Pipeline First
narrative.text: Before writing a single line of the actual problem, the exact tool chain — a Singularity container running Fast Downward — was verified against a real competition task, pulled directly from the official IPC 2018 repository, rather than trusted blindly.

narrative.label: Modeling the Problem
narrative.text: The rover's world becomes three PDDL actions: move between connected locations, pick up a mineral, deliver it to any location marked as a lab — deliberately generic, never hardcoded to one specific lab.

narrative.label: Solving It — Provably
narrative.text: Run against the real path network from the brief, the planner doesn't just find a route — it proves this is the shortest one possible: 14 steps, mathematically optimal.
narrative.caption: The real directional path network from the problem brief.

narrative.label: Scaling It Up, Without Touching the Model
narrative.text: Two new scenarios were added — another mineral and site, then a second lab entirely — and the exact same domain file solved both. Zero modifications to the model itself.
narrative.caption: Optimal plan length across three growing scenarios — same domain.pddl, unchanged.

narrative.label: The Interesting Part
narrative.text: In the hardest scenario, with two labs available, the planner independently chose to deliver each mineral to whichever lab was actually closer — proof the model generalizes on its own, rather than happening to work by coincidence.

narrative.label: Why Delfi 1 Isn't Here
narrative.text: The actual IPC 2018 champion planner, Delfi 1, is honestly unreachable today: its container lived on Singularity Hub (shut down in 2021), its source on a Mercurial repository (Bitbucket dropped Mercurial support in 2020). Since Delfi 1 is itself built on Fast Downward, this project runs Fast Downward directly — with the same optimality guarantee the competition's own optimal track requires.

pipeline: 🗺️ Modeling: PDDL domain — move / pick-up / deliver, generic over any number of labs
🧪 Pipeline validation: real IPC 2018 benchmark task (Snake), solved in 24 optimal steps
🪨 Problem 1: base scenario — 2 minerals, 1 lab — 14 optimal steps
🔬 Problem 3: +1 mineral, +1 lab — 18 optimal steps, planner chose the nearer lab per delivery
✅ Validation: every plan cross-checked against a second, independent planner
study.code_spotlight:
(:action deliver
    :parameters (?rover ?mineral ?loc)
    :precondition
    (and
        (at ?rover ?loc)
        (carrying ?rover ?mineral)
        (LAB ?loc)
    )
    :effect
    (and
        (analyzed ?mineral)
        (not (carrying ?rover ?mineral))
        (free ?rover)
    )
)

; Run to provable optimality:
; fast-downward.sif domain.pddl problem3.pddl --search "astar(lmcut())"
; -> Plan cost: 18 (optimal) -- planner delivers to whichever LAB is closer

solutions.title: Custom Certification & Training Platform
solutions.description: Many companies need to train teams on a specific tool, internal process, or compliance topic — and generic courses don't cover that. This is a self-paced trainer with spaced-repetition scheduling, built to turn any body of knowledge into a certification-style question bank that actually sticks, instead of a slide deck nobody reopens. I originally built it to stay sharp on my own technical fundamentals — because in this field, you either keep training or you fall behind.
